onestepcox

onestepcox computes closed-form estimators of the hazard ratio of a two-group comparison of survival data that approximate the Cox partial likelihood estimator without iteration. The proposed estimator starts from the Mantel-Haenszel estimator and takes one Halley step on the Cox score equation. Its standard error is updated in the same pass over the risk sets, and a Wald confidence interval is returned. The Efron and Breslow handling of tied event times and stratification are supported. The package is written in R only.

The documentation, with the reference manual and the vignettes, is at https://gosukehommaex.github.io/onestepcox/.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("gosukehommaEX/onestepcox")

The vignettes describe the estimators, their agreement with the survival package, simulations, and the large-sample limits. To build them, install with remotes::install_github("gosukehommaEX/onestepcox", build_vignettes = TRUE) and see browseVignettes("onestepcox").

Methods of EstHR()

method Estimator of the log hazard ratio
"MH_Halley" Proposed: Mantel-Haenszel anchor and one Halley step
"MH_Newton", "MH_Chebyshev" Mantel-Haenszel anchor and one Newton or Chebyshev step
"Pike_Halley", "Pike_Newton", "Pike_Chebyshev" Pike anchor and one Halley, Newton, or Chebyshev step
"MH", "Pike", "Peto" Closed-form estimators
"Cox" Cox estimate by survival::coxph() with a tight tolerance
"Cox_NR" Cox estimate by Newton-Raphson iteration on the same risk-set summaries as the closed-form estimators

Every method returns coef, exp(coef), se(coef), and the confidence limits, named as in summary() of a coxph fit; several methods at once give a matrix with one row per method. RiskTable() returns the risk-set summaries (numbers at risk and events at each distinct event time) that all methods except "Cox" share.

The data are given by a formula Surv(time, event) ~ group + strata(s) and a data frame, as in survival::coxph(), or as vectors. With a formula, the control group is the first level of the group variable (or its smallest value) unless control is given, and rows with missing values are removed.

Example 

library(onestepcox)
est <- EstHR(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon, data = survival::gbsg,
             method = c("MH_Halley", "Pike", "Peto", "Cox"))
est        # print(): groups, estimates, z, p-values, and intervals
plot(est)  # forest plot of the hazard ratios

# Breslow ties and strata by tumor grade
EstHR(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon + strata(grade), data = survival::gbsg,
      method = "MH_Halley", ties = "breslow")

# The same estimate from vectors
d <- survival::gbsg
EstHR(d$rfstime, d$status, d$hormon, control = 0, method = "MH_Halley",
      ties = "breslow", strata = d$grade)

# Risk-set summaries
head(RiskTable(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon, data = survival::gbsg))

The plot() methods of EstHR(), CompareOC(), and LimitHR() results draw with ggplot2 and return a ggplot object, which can be changed further with ggplot2 (for example plot(est) + ggplot2::theme(...)) or saved with ggplot2::ggsave(). They take the labels of the methods (labels; by default the method names with hyphens, such as MH-Halley), the colors (col), point shapes and sizes (shape, size), line types and widths (linetype, linewidth), the base font size in points (base_size), and the position of the legend (legend_pos: "bottom", "top", "right", or "left" outside the panel, coordinates c(x, y) inside it, or "none"). The legend is below the panel by default, except in the forest plot of EstHR(), where the methods label the vertical axis.

Simulation and large-sample limits

GenSimData() generates two-group trials with exponential survival times, uniform accrual, optional dropout, and an analysis at a fixed number of events, optionally with strata that have their own baseline hazards and with times rounded up to a unit (which produces ties). CompareOC() runs GenSimData() and EstHR() over a set of scenarios and reports, for each method, the distribution of the deviation from a reference (by default the Cox estimate), also relative to the standard error of the reference, the proportion of replicates in which the hazard ratio with two decimals differs from that of the reference, the ratio of the standard errors, the bias, standard deviation, RMSE, mean standard error, and coverage relative to the true hazard ratio, and the computing time.

LimitHR() computes the limits of the estimators as the sample size grows under the design of GenSimData(). The Mantel-Haenszel and Cox estimators converge to the true log hazard ratio, whereas the Pike and Peto estimators, and the one-step corrections from the Pike anchor, converge to other values.

lim <- LimitHR(HR = c(0.5, 2, 10), hazard_C = log(2) / 18,
               n_T = 100, n_C = 100, a = 12, E = 160)
lim        # bias by method and hazard ratio
plot(lim)  # absolute bias against the hazard ratio

Tests, reproduction, and validation

The tests compare the closed-form estimators, the score derivatives, the risk-set summaries, and the large-sample limits with values computed beforehand by an independent Python implementation (tools/test_expected/, not part of the package build), and compare "Cox" and "Cox_NR" with survival::coxph().

inst/reproduce/ reproduces published results: Figure 1 of Berry, Kitchin and Mock (1991) (Peto and Pike estimates in simulated trials) and the closed-form results for test data 1 of Therneau and Grambsch (2000). inst/validation/ compares all estimators with an independent Python implementation on 203 datasets and LimitHR() with simulations of 100,000 subjects. Each script writes its checks to a results/ folder, and inst/validation/summarize_validation.R counts them.
